md: Kernel-side data (EPROCESS, and the VADs of the next lesson) is what the process cannot easily edit; user-side data (PEB, loader lists, command line) is what it can. When they disagree, believe the kernel side and ask why the user side was changed.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
md: Fragmentation is not a leak. In a leak, *live* data grows because the program forgets to free. With fragmentation, live data is flat while the *footprint* grows. Tell them apart by comparing the bytes the allocator says are allocated with the memory it holds: a leak raises both, fragmentation widens the gap.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Relaxed: one agreed history per variable, nothing more
md: Myth: "Relaxed writes may take ages to show up, and SeqCst makes them visible sooner." The memory model says nothing about timing at all, only about order. A stronger ordering does not make data travel faster; it may even slow your program down.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
md: Holding a guard is holding back everyone's garbage. Pinning across a blocking call, a lock wait or a long iteration stops the epoch from advancing for all threads. crossbeam provides `Guard::repin` to briefly unpin and pin again inside long loops; references loaded before the repin are no longer protected.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Where things live: code, static data, heap and stack
md: The bug class tells you how memory is misused; the region tells you what gets damaged. Stack overflows threaten return addresses, heap overflows threaten neighbouring objects and allocator data.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
md: A subtle limit of contrastive loss: it pulls every same-identity pair toward distance 0, so it tries to squash all images of one person onto a single point. The authors of FaceNet (Google's 2015 face recognition system, next lesson) argued that a triplet loss is better suited, because it only asks same-identity images to be closer than other identities, letting one person's images spread out along a region.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: When the optimizer deletes the code you meant to time
md: Misconception: "returning or summing the result is enough". Using the output defeats dead-code elimination, but not constant folding. The input must also come from somewhere the compiler cannot see through. JMH's constant-folding sample says to read inputs from non-final fields of a state object, and warns against making them `final` even when your IDE suggests it.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
md: The Miles docs do not publish a line-by-line diff against slime. This course teaches what Miles documents and measures; do not conclude from it that slime lacks any particular feature.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Low-precision RL: formats, scales and the precision contract
md: TITO fixes which tokens are trained on, R3 fixes which experts process them, and the precision contract fixes how each matmul is quantized. Each removes one cause of the importance ratio drifting away from 1.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
md: The **good decision ratio** (good evictions divided by all evictions) grades each eviction individually. The LRB authors found it correlates strongly with the final byte miss ratio, so they used it to choose features, model, loss and sizes from one simulation pass instead of hours-long full simulations per design.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Dynamic instrumentation with Frida: watch and change a running app
md: On a device its user controls, any value in the app's memory and any boolean the app computes can be read and changed. Design so that changing them gains nothing: keys in secure hardware, decisions on the server.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why per-head keys and values make the KV cache huge
md: The paper counts cache size in **elements**, regardless of storage precision. Quantizing the cache, storing each element in fewer bits such as FP8 (an 8-bit floating-point format) or lower, is a separate, stackable trick. When comparing headline numbers, check whether both sides use the same precision.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Why MLA can beat GQA at equal cache, and converting models
md: At equal cache, GQA is MLA with selector up-projections, so MLA can only add expressiveness. Converting a trained model to MLA means confining RoPE to a small part, compressing the rest into a latent, and fine-tuning briefly.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: The multi-query pipeline: generate, retrieve in parallel, merge
md: LangChain's synchronous `invoke` searches the generated queries **one after another** in a for loop; only the async `ainvoke` path runs them concurrently with `asyncio.gather`. LlamaIndex runs them concurrently when `use_async=True` (its default). If your multi-query latency grows linearly with N, check which path you are on.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Latency budgets and phased ranking in real engines
md: Defaults are shallow. Both Elasticsearch's rescore window_size and text_similarity_reranker's rank_window_size default to 10, so an unconfigured reranker can only shuffle the first page. Also keep the window fixed across pages: the docs warn that changing window_size while paginating can make top hits shift.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why a weight matrix is not a bag of independent numbers
md: Treat a weight matrix as a linear map, not a list of numbers. Its gradient has directions with very different strengths, and these optimizers rebalance those directions instead of rebalancing individual entries.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Scaling Muon to LLMs: weight decay, update RMS and QK-clip
md: Both Moonlight fixes control the *size* of Muon's update, not its direction: decay keeps weights from drifting out of bf16's precise range, and 0.2 sqrt(max(A, B)) gives every matrix the same update RMS as AdamW. QK-clip then caps the one quantity, attention logits, that still grew.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why 'maximal': kernel, mean-field and feature-learning limits
md: The dichotomy is about the limit as width goes to infinity. A finite SP network does learn features (the paper says so explicitly). The problem is the trend: as you widen an SP model at a stable learning rate, its feature learning fades, and the optimum HPs move. muP keeps feature learning the same at every width, which is why its HPs transfer.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What muP does not transfer: horizon, weight decay, the SP debate
md: "Per-layer SP beat muP" does not mean muP is wrong. Everett et al. also tune per-layer constants at small scale and transfer them, with per-layer LR exponents; the debate is about which exponents and alignment assumptions hold in practice. Both camps agree that one global LR with SP init is the thing that does not transfer.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices
md: User-space spin locks lack the kernel's guarantee. A user thread cannot disable preemption, so a pure spin lock in an application can always spin against a preempted holder. Prefer the platform mutex, which already spins briefly before sleeping.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
md: Snapshot isolation prevents conflicts between writes to the same row. Write skew slips through because the conflicting pair is a read and a write to *different* rows.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Transformer taggers and subword alignment
md:
Two alignment bugs cost real F1 and neither one crashes.

Labelling continuation pieces with `I-X` instead of -100 teaches the model that spans can start and continue inside a word, which leaks into the decoder.

Evaluating on pieces instead of words changes the number of gold entities, so your F1 is not comparable to anyone else's. Map back to words first, then score.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Why MD5 misses copies, and the average hash that does not
md: A perceptual hash is a summary you **compare**, not an identity you **look up**. Similar images give hashes at a small Hamming distance; the system decides a threshold for what counts as a match.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: a custom environment and dataset for GRPO
md: Rewards add up across turns: the rollout does `reward_dict[name][active_indices] += r` on every turn. This variant pays `reward/format` on both turns, so a reply that needed the hint ends with correctness 1 and format 2, a total of 3, more than a first-try success (1 and 1). The model is paid to miss once. Return zeros on non-final turns, or score only when you terminate.

courseTitle: Network attacks and defences
lessonTitle: BGP hijacks and route leaks: the MyEtherWallet case
md: A BGP hijack does not need to touch your servers or your users' networks. It moves traffic somewhere else on the internet, where your TLS certificate, DNSSEC signatures and user training are the remaining defences.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Packets, flows and logs: three kinds of network evidence
md: Packets are the most complete evidence and the most expensive to keep. Logs and flows are what you will actually have for anything older than a few days, so design your monitoring around the questions you will need to answer months later.

courseTitle: Network traffic analysis: Wireshark, Zeek and Suricata
lessonTitle: Case: hunting Cobalt Strike servers by certificate, JARM and quirks
md: Hunt with layers: a cheap exact indicator (default serial, OpenSSL default subject), a fingerprint of the software (JA3S, JA4S, JARM), and behaviour (timing, rarity, newly seen servers). Each layer catches what the others miss, and corroboration turns leads into findings.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Ethernet frames and MAC addresses
md: A MAC address is not an identity. Operating systems let you change it, [Android](https://source.android.com/docs/core/connect/wifi-mac-randomization) uses a randomized address per Wi-Fi network by default since Android 10, and it never leaves the local link: routers replace it at every hop. "Allow only these MAC addresses" stops honest mistakes, not attackers.

courseTitle: How networks work, seen by an attacker and a defender
lessonTitle: Reading a packet capture like a defender
md: Captures contain other people's data: passwords, messages, cookies. Capture only on networks and machines you own or are explicitly authorised to monitor, keep the files protected, and delete them when done. Intercepting others' traffic without authorisation is illegal in most countries (the security basics course covers the law).

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
md: Good NUMA placement does two things at once: it keeps misses local (latency) and it spreads traffic over every memory controller (bandwidth). Losing either one can cost more than the latency penalty alone suggests.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
md: NMS is not learned and does not look at the image. It only sees boxes and scores. It cannot remove a confident false positive that overlaps nothing (B3), and in dense scenes it removes real objects that happen to overlap.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
md: Object storage is cheap, durable and shared, which makes compute stateless. The price is high per-request latency and a per-request fee. Everything else follows from batching writes and caching reads to pay that price rarely.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Inside a classic histogram: buckets, cumulative counts, interpolation
md: A classic histogram quantile is an interpolation inside one bucket. Its error is bounded by that bucket's width and nothing else, so a percentile panel is only as good as the boundary you placed next to the value you care about.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
md: CTC adds a blank symbol and a collapse rule (merge repeats, then drop blanks). That lets a recognizer train from whole-line transcripts with no character positions, and the blank is what makes double letters possible.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Discretionary vs mandatory access control, and the LSM hooks
md: MAC limits damage; it does not remove bugs. The SELinux Notebook is blunt: SELinux "will not stop memory leaks or buffer over-runs" and "will not stop kernel vulnerabilities", though it may contain their effects. A policy also cannot stop anything it allows.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Putting it together: one service, many layers
md: Assume each layer will fail and ask what the next one still guarantees: least privilege inside the program (privsep, drops), MAC around it, seccomp and capabilities on its kernel access, namespaces and cgroups around its view, and a separate kernel when the code is hostile. Patching is the layer under all of them.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Search operators: asking a search engine precise questions
md: Operators filter the search engine's copy, not the site. They are cheap and silent, which is why defenders should run them against themselves first.

courseTitle: OSINT: open-source intelligence, done ethically
lessonTitle: Case: MH17 and the open-source trail of a missile launcher
md: MH17 is the model: geolocate each item, chronolocate it with independent methods, fingerprint the object, state the limits, and let formal investigators test it.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
md: A common misconception is that editing a `.h` file only affects the `.cpp` with the same name. The compiler pastes headers into every includer, so `tensor.h` here costs 4 recompiles, not 1.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Running exactly the tests that matter with pytest
md: Node ids, `-k`, `-m` and `--lf` turn a 20 minute suite into a 2 second loop. Use the narrow loop while fixing, then run the wider set CI will run before you push.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Answering review comments as the author
md: Answer every comment, say what you changed, fix the code rather than explaining it in the thread, and thank the reviewer. The kernel guide adds: when you send a new version, list what changed since the previous one.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
md: A CoC is not only about insults. Contributor Covenant 2.1 lists publishing others' private information (an address, an email) without explicit permission as unacceptable, and it covers private harassment too.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup
md: Fixup commits are not magic on their own. If you push `fixup!` commits and never autosquash, a PR merged with a merge commit or with rebase and merge (two of GitHub's merge methods, covered in lesson 5) lands them on main exactly as they are, `fixup!` titles and all. Autosquash before asking for the final merge unless the project says otherwise.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom
md: Two common myths: copyleft does not make internal use public (only conveying triggers it), and it does not ban commercial use (you may charge for copies). What it controls is the terms you pass on.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
md: Common misconception: "the new number is smaller, so the change is faster". Two single measurements differ almost always, even for identical code. Without repeated runs and a test, a 5% gap can be pure noise.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Trace one request: a Redis GET from socket to reply
md: Trace from the specific end toward the general one. Start at the observable string or the command's own handler, search downward through callees, and use a backtrace (or a log line) to bridge function pointers, callbacks and event loops.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: git bisect: finding the commit that introduced the bug
md: Do not reuse a reducer's interestingness script as a bisect script unchanged. They use opposite conventions: for C-Reduce and llvm-reduce, exit 0 means the bug is *present*; for `git bisect run`, exit 0 means the commit is *good* (bug absent). The inversion silently sends bisect to the wrong commit.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: A title and description that explain why
md: Do not write `Closes #123` on a PR that only partly addresses the issue: merging it will close the issue for everyone. Write "Part of #123" or "Refs #123" (neither is a closing keyword).

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Automatic prefix caching in vLLM: hashing full blocks
md: Only **full** blocks are cached. If two prompts share 10 tokens and the block size is 16, nothing is reused. Lookup also always starts from block 0: a shared passage in the middle of two prompts gives no hit, because its KV depends on everything before it.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Passive recon: certificate logs, search engines and leaked code
md: A leaked password or API key found during recon is not an invitation to log in with it. Unless the rules of engagement explicitly allow using discovered credentials, record where it was found and report it at once so it can be rotated.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Reading a flame graph: width, top edges and plateaus
md: Colors carry no meaning in a default CPU flame graph. Gregg picks random warm colors only to separate neighbors. Other palettes exist (for example coloring kernel, user and just-in-time (JIT) frames differently, where JIT code is machine code that a runtime such as the Java virtual machine compiles while the program runs), but never read hotness from hue.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Flushes, fences and the order things become durable
md: A fence without a flush does nothing for durability on ADR platforms, and a flush without a fence gives no ordering: CLWB and CLFLUSHOPT are not ordered with each other or with later stores. You need both, in the order store, flush, fence, then the dependent store.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: DMARC: alignment, policy and reports
md: Misconception: "we have DMARC, so we are protected from phishing". DMARC at p=reject stops exact-domain spoofing of **your** domain. It does nothing against lookalike domains, display-name spoofs or a compromised real mailbox, and p=none stops nothing at all; it only reports.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Shrinking a struct by reordering its fields
md: Do not reorder blindly. If a struct's layout is part of a file format, a network protocol, a hardware register map or an ABI shared with other code, changing the order changes the bytes and breaks every reader. Reordering is safe only for structs that are private to one build of your program.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Heatmaps: training targets, argmax and sub-pixel decoding
md: The network never outputs coordinates. It outputs heatmaps, and a small hand-written decoder (argmax, quarter-cell shift, scale by stride, undo the crop) turns them into numbers. Bugs in that decoder, such as swapping x and y or forgetting the crop offset, look like a bad model.

courseTitle: Post-quantum cryptography and migration
lessonTitle: Encrypting one bit with LWE, by hand
md: This toy exists to make the math visible. Never write your own lattice cryptography for real use: use ML-KEM from a maintained library (lesson 8), whose implementers also handle constant-time code, input checks and randomness.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
md: Do not read 3% as a safe threshold. Proximity graphs are not random graphs, matching nodes are often clustered, and being connected is weaker than being *navigable*: greedy search can stall in a matching region long before the subgraph formally splits. Qdrant's docs simply warn that the HNSW graph starts to fall apart when filters are too strict.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: What privacy engineering protects, beyond keeping secrets
md: "Encrypted, access-controlled and never breached" is a security result, not a privacy result. A system can meet every confidentiality control and still harm people through what it does by design with the data: publishing, combining, inferring or keeping it.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: k-anonymity: generalise and suppress until you hide in a crowd
md: k-anonymity: every combination of quasi-identifier values appears at least k times, achieved by generalising and suppressing. Its strength depends entirely on choosing the right quasi-identifiers and on every other release made from the same data.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Differential privacy in real systems: units, trust and hazards
md: Check every DP claim for its unit of privacy (event or user), its trust model (central, local or in between), its epsilon and delta (delta at most 1 / n squared), and its implementation (a vetted library, not hand-written noise).

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Secure aggregation: a server that learns only the sum
md: Secure aggregation: pairwise masks that cancel in the sum hide each value from the server; secret sharing handles dropouts; double masking stops a server from faking dropouts. The total is still revealed, so require many contributors and add DP noise when the total must not identify anyone.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: Linux escalation 2: jobs, scripts and paths that root trusts
md: The same rule covers the files that define privilege themselves. A writable `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/sudoers.d/` entry or systemd unit directory is instant root. Treat any group or world write bit under `/etc` or `/usr` as a finding.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Build it: train a small PRM and rerank with it
md: Tokenize each step separately and append the separator id yourself. In the Qwen2.5 tokenizer a step ending in a period followed by a newline becomes the single token for period-plus-newline (id 624), so tokenizing the joined text gives no separate newline token to read, and the label would sit on a different token than at training time.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a process owns and what a thread shares
md: A process is a **resource container** (memory, files, handlers); a thread is an **execution stream** (PC, registers, stack). Threads in one process see each other's writes; separate processes do not, unless they set up sharing on purpose.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
md: The one number to remember is not the microseconds of a single switch but **switches per second times total cost per switch**, where total includes the cache and TLB refill. Keep CPU-bound threads near the core count, and reserve extra threads or async I/O for work that actually waits.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Worked example: selecting a prompt and the winner's curse
md: The data that chose the prompt cannot also grade it. Report the selected prompt's score on a held-out set that played no part in any choice, and expect it to be lower than the dev score.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Text versus bytes: what a computer actually stores
md: Do not "fix" decode errors with `errors="ignore"` in security tooling. It silently deletes the bad bytes, so `ad\xffmin` becomes `admin` and your report shows a username the attacker never sent. Prefer `replace`, which leaves a visible mark.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Encodings: base64, hex and URL encoding, and why attackers use them
md: Never decode and then *run* what you decoded to see what it does. Decode to text, read it, and search it. Executing an unknown PowerShell or shell command, even in your own terminal, is how an analyst becomes the next victim. Use an isolated analysis sandbox if you truly need behaviour.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Relevance feedback: Rocchio, pseudo-relevance feedback and RM3
md: Feedback is only as good as its top k. When the first-pass top results are relevant, PRF finds words the user never typed; when they are off-topic, it amplifies the error. On MS MARCO dev, the query2doc paper reports BM25 MRR@10 18.4 against 15.8 for BM25 + RM3, while recall@1k rose slightly (85.7 to 86.4).

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: RaBitQ indexing: normalize, rotate randomly, keep the signs
md: The rotation does not make every vector quantize well on every draw. It makes the quality *random with a known distribution*, the same for every input direction. That is what turns "works on my dataset" into a guarantee that holds regardless of the data.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Discounts, refunds and rewards: value that can be claimed twice
md: Evaluate every reward rule against the final state of the transaction, at the moment value moves, and record each grant so it cannot be granted again. A rule checked earlier is a rule that can go stale.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Fixing races in the database: atomic updates, locks, constraints
md: "It is in a transaction" is not a race fix by itself. At Read Committed, a SELECT then an UPDATE in one transaction still race. You need a lock, a conditional write, a constraint, or SERIALIZABLE with retries.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Why replicas need consensus, and why majorities work
md: Majorities intersect. Every safety argument in Paxos and Raft comes down to one server that sat in both quorums and remembered what it saw.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Top-k, the token budget, and where chunks sit in the prompt
md: Three separate decisions shape the context: **how many** chunks (top-k), **how many tokens** they may use (the budget, set by the window minus everything else), and **in what order** they appear. Tune them together; raising k without a budget or an ordering rule mostly adds noise to the middle.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
md: **Recall@k is not Success@k.** Some papers report "Recall@k" meaning *at least one relevant document is in the top k*. The ir_measures documentation calls that **Success@k** and reserves R@k for the fraction of all relevant documents retrieved. For q1 every run has Success@5 = 1, while R@5 ranges from 0.167 to 0.667. Check which one a paper means before comparing numbers.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Extortion layers: encryption, theft, leak sites and pressure
md: Backups defeat encryption only. Stolen data is lost the moment it leaves, so treat exfiltration detection as part of ransomware defence, and prepare the communication that answers a leak-site post before one appears.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Recovery sequencing: identity first, then the business
md: Recover in dependency order: a clean network, then the independent backup system, then identity restored in isolation from a pre-attack backup with privileged secrets reset, then security tooling, then business services by a critical asset list agreed before the incident.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: WebSocket: one HTTP upgrade, then a two-way framed stream
md: Masking is **not encryption**: the key travels in the same frame. RFC 6455 requires it (even over TLS) so that a script in the browser cannot choose the exact bytes on the wire. Without it, an attacker could craft upgraded traffic that a broken proxy reads as an HTTP request and caches, then serves that forged response to other users: the cache-poisoning attack in section 10.3. Use `wss://` (TLS) for confidentiality.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: From a sparse rating matrix to item-to-item recommendations
md: Item-to-item CF scales because the heavy work (the similar-items table) is offline, and the online step only touches the handful of items in one user's history.

courseTitle: Measuring size from a reference marker
lessonTitle: Why a photo has no scale until you add a reference
md: A reference object gives you scale only for points at its depth (more precisely, on its plane). Everything else in the image has a different pixels-per-mm.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: How the planner chooses: join order search and row estimates
md: The same study found that most of PostgreSQL's timeouts came from a nested-loop join without an index, chosen because a tiny row estimate made it look cheapest. When the real input was large, its rows x rows work exploded. A cost-only choice ignores how risky a plan is if the estimate is wrong.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
md: The reward is an imperfect measurement of the goal. Optimization pressure flows to wherever the measurement and the goal disagree, so the harder you optimize, the more those disagreements decide what you get.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: From gaming to tampering: reward tampering and in-context hacking
md: Gaming generalizes. A model rewarded for easy, harmless-looking gaming became more likely to try rarer and more blatant gaming it was never trained on, and training away only the gaming you can see leaves some of the rest.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Monte Carlo: simulating 100,000 years of losses
md: Monte Carlo is not magic: garbage ranges give precise-looking garbage. The model also assumes the factors are independent (here, a bad attack year does not make secondary losses bigger), which may not hold. Show your inputs with the outputs, say what is assumed, and rerun when estimates change. Simplified: real FAIR tools also model multiple loss forms separately and correlations between factors.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: ISO/IEC 27001: an ISMS, Annex A and the certification audit
md: ISO 27001 certifies a management system: risk assessment, treatment, a Statement of Applicability against 93 Annex A controls, internal audit, management review, continual improvement. Certificates last three years with yearly surveillance. The SoA and your risk register are the documents everything else hangs from.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Breach notification clocks and US disclosure rules
md: Know your clocks before the incident: NIS2 24 h and 72 h, GDPR 72 h from awareness, SEC four business days from a materiality decision made without unreasonable delay, state laws often 30 to 60 days, HIPAA at most 60 days. Encryption is an exemption almost everywhere. Prepare templates and decision owners in the incident plan.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
md: Rollout is the bottleneck. FLOPs are dominated by training, but wall-clock time is dominated by sequential decoding. Most RL infrastructure ideas (fast inference engines, placement, resharding, asynchrony, partial rollouts) are ways to make generation faster or to keep the other GPUs busy while it runs.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Asynchronous RL: staleness, importance ratios and the speedup
md: Asynchrony converts idle GPU time into staleness. Every async system pairs a staleness bound (versions tracked per trajectory) with an objective that knows which policy sampled each token: an importance weight from behavior to proximal policy, and a trust region around a recent policy.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Ceilings, hierarchical rooflines and Nsight Compute
md: Read the gaps. In the NERSC study of DeepCAM (a deep learning model that finds extreme weather patterns in climate images), a kernel whose L1, L2 and HBM points sit close together shows a streaming pattern with poor cache locality; a large gap between the L2 and HBM points shows that L2 misses were rare. The binding level is the one whose roof is lowest at that level's own intensity.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: How k shapes the curve 1/(k + r)
md: At the default k = 60 with typical windows (tens of results), RRF behaves like a vote count first (how many lists returned the document) and uses ranks mainly to order documents with the same count. Smaller k gives ranks more say; larger k makes it closer to pure vote counting.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Build, load and test a Rust module
md: Misconception: "an `assert!` in a kernel doctest panics the kernel." In doctests and `#[kunit_tests]` modules the assert macros are replaced with versions that report to KUnit and do not panic. That is also why tests should use `?` instead of `unwrap()`: an `unwrap()` on `Err` is a real panic, and the kernel's panic handler calls `BUG()`, which reports a fatal kernel error (more in lesson 3).

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The baseline you replace: EEVDF picks and the knobs it offers
md: EEVDF in one line: weight sets the share, the requested slice sets the latency, and eligibility keeps any task from running far ahead of its share. A BPF scheduler gets none of this for free; lesson 5 shows the minimal one getting weights only partly right.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Build, load and run your own scheduler end to end
md: A scheduler is two programs: a BPF object (callbacks plus maps, gathered in one `sched_ext_ops` struct_ops map) and a loader that opens it, sets read-only options, loads, attaches, polls and reports why it exited. Exiting the loader is the unload.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Measuring and debugging a scheduler
md: Measure percentiles, not means; A/B on one kernel, alternating runs, and report the spread. Then verify the nice and cgroup controls you depend on, because each scheduler decides which ones it honors.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Rotation without outages: overlap, versions and staged labels
md: Rotation that nobody watches fails silently. Alert on rotation failures, on keys older than their cryptoperiod, and on authentication failures right after a rotation (a consumer that missed the switch). The Storm-0558 key in the next lesson survived because rotation had stopped and nothing alerted on its age.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Python: archives, asserts, temp files and what Bandit sees
md: Python review checklist from lessons 3 and 4: no eval/exec/pickle/unsafe YAML on outside data; archive extraction with filter='data' and size limits; no assert for security; mkstemp or NamedTemporaryFile, never mktemp; secrets for tokens and compare_digest for comparisons; and a manual trace for every path.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Apple goto fail: one duplicated line in C
md: When reviewing C control flow, read the braces, not the indentation, and ask: if this function exits early, what does it return? A security check must fail closed: the only path to "success" should be the one that passed every check.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Writing the finding and the fix so it gets merged
md: A finding is complete when a developer can act on it alone: what is wrong (line and CWE), why it matters (impact and who can reach it), how you know (a safe reproduction), how to fix the class (code), and how to keep it fixed (a regression test that fails on the old code).

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: Blast-RADIUS (CVE-2024-3596): MD5 collisions turn Reject into Accept
md: The bug was not "MD5 is old" alone. It was MD5 in a construction that let a collision survive the secret (secret at the end), plus a protocol rule that let the attacker plant bytes inside the authenticated reply. Keyed constructions like HMAC, and authenticating the whole channel with TLS, remove both.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Assurance: the Orange Book, Common Criteria and what they prove
md: "EAL4 certified" on a datasheet tells you how hard the evaluators looked, not what they looked at. The answer to "certified for what?" is in the security target, and it may exclude the very feature you are buying the product for.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: SASE, SSE and the cloud edge: SD-WAN, SWG, CASB and FWaaS
md: SASE is a delivery model, not a new control. Underneath it are the same enforcement points as before (firewall, web filter, CASB, ZTNA), moved from your data centre to someone else's points of presence.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: LLM-assisted triage: the model advises, code and people decide
md: A suggestion field that accepts free text will eventually contain an action, a threat or an instruction. Constrain it to a fixed set of values and treat everything else as a failed reply.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Threat, vulnerability, exploit, payload and risk
md: Vulnerability = the weakness. Threat = who or what could use it. Exploit = the act or code that uses it. Payload = what runs afterwards. Risk = likelihood times impact. You remove risk by fixing vulnerabilities, reducing exposure, or reducing impact (backups, and segmentation: splitting a network into zones that cannot freely reach each other).

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Equifax 2017: a known bug and a missed patch
md: Equifax failed at the boring basics: inventory, patch tracking, credential storage, segmentation and monitoring health. No single failure caused the breach; every layer had a hole, which is the subject of lesson 10.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: What a security leader is for: the CISO's job and reporting line
md: A security leader sets direction, secures resources, makes risk visible to its owners and leads in crises. The reporting line should keep information flowing to the decision makers without a filter or a conflict of interest.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Vendors and tools: buy, build, consolidate and plan the exit
md: Retire tools that add nothing unique, but only after checking depth, retention and what was built on them. Buy common capabilities, build only where you are different, outsource what you cannot staff, and treat every critical vendor as a concentration risk with an exit plan.

courseTitle: Security leadership: strategy, programmes and teams
lessonTitle: Regulators and disclosure: materiality, risk factors, certifications
md: The CISO feeds facts and unknowns into the disclosure process fast, signs only sub-certifications the records support, keeps risk factors honest about what has already happened, and knows each regulator's clock and who signs what.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Case: Storm-0558, a corrected blog and the CSRB report
md: When an earlier statement turns out wrong, correct it publicly, quickly and visibly, and say what changed. Readers make decisions on what you wrote; leaving an error standing keeps those decisions wrong.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: STaR and ReST-EM: sample, keep what is correct, fine-tune
md: Each STaR iteration fine-tunes the **original** pretrained model on the new dataset, not the previous checkpoint, to avoid overfitting. ReST-EM does the same and reports much better transfer to held-out tasks than continuing from the last iteration. The model improves through better data, not through stacked training runs.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Why exact-match caches miss, and how a semantic cache matches meaning
md: A semantic cache trades exactness for hit rate. An exact cache never returns an answer to a different question; a semantic cache does so by design whenever two questions are close enough. The rest of this course is about where "close enough" goes wrong.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Why cloud metadata is the prize: Capital One 2019
md: "It is in a private subnet" does not protect a role's credentials. Temporary credentials from IMDS work from anywhere on the internet unless a policy restricts where they can be used. The attacker used them from their own machine.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: LM programs: why the runtime should see the whole program
md: Misconception: "SGLang is a prompt DSL, so I must rewrite my app to use it." A DSL, or domain-specific language, is a small language built for one kind of job, here writing LM programs. Most of SGLang's speedups live in the runtime and apply to plain HTTP requests. The DSL is an optional layer on top.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
md: In practice the straight-line bound is weak on real road networks with travel times: it must divide by the top motorway speed, so it badly underestimates slow city streets. The Bast et al. survey reports the gain is small or nonexistent. **ALT** gets much better bounds from precomputed distances to a few landmarks plus the triangle inequality.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: The FFT: from N squared to N log N with butterflies
md: The FFT is not an approximation. It returns the same numbers as the DFT matrix product, up to floating point rounding, by sharing work through $\log_2 N$ stages of $N/2$ butterflies.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
md: Misconception: "SVE code is written for a particular width like 512 bits." VLA code must never assume a length; use svcntw() and whilelt. ACLE warns that something like `svptrue_pat_b32(SV_VL16)` loads no data at all on chips narrower than 512 bits.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: How Linux stacks them, and how to choose
md: A pool or arena that never returns memory looks like a leak from the outside. Bonwick's caches give memory back under memory pressure, when the virtual memory system runs short of free pages; your custom pool should have some way to shrink (reset, trim, or a size cap).

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Generating data: the rollout loop and your own functions
md: Put per-sample agent logic in a custom generate function and scoring in a custom reward function. You keep slime's batching, dynamic sampling, abort and partial-rollout machinery for free, and your code works unchanged under fully async rollout.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: What a SOC is, and what an analyst does all day
md: An alert is a question, not an answer. The analyst's job is to answer it with evidence, record the answer so someone else can check it, and feed what was learned back into the rules.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Phishing reports and unusual data egress
md: Volume alone is a weak signal; volume against the host's own baseline, plus the sending process and the destination's owner, is a strong one. Exfiltration to a popular cloud storage service will look normal by destination, so the process and the account doing the upload matter most.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Warnings people heed: browser warnings and opinionated design
md: Warnings work when they are rare, specific and opinionated, and fail when they are frequent and neutral. Where the safe answer is always the same, block instead of warning.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Dropped USB drives, implants and unattended screens
md: Misconception: "it's only dangerous if someone opens a file on the drive". Devices that present themselves as a keyboard can type commands as soon as they are connected, and a network implant needs no user action at all. Controls must act at connection time.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Training at scale: dead latents and feature splitting
md: Dead latents grow with width; fix them with resampling, encoder-equals-decoder-transpose init and an AuxK loss. Feature splitting means the dictionary you get depends on width, so a feature is always 'a feature at this resolution'.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Build it yourself: train a TopK SAE on GPT-2, then use a released one
md: A working SAE pipeline is: cache a site with BOS dropped, shuffle, normalise by one scalar, train with transposed init and unit decoder columns (plus AuxK at scale), then judge it by L0, FVU and delta LM loss from splicing. A released SAE plus Neuronpedia gets you to reading and steering in a few lines.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
md: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in 2D or 3D coordinates. Simple kriging is the zero-mean GP on residuals; ordinary kriging adds an unknown constant mean; universal kriging adds trend basis functions; the nugget is observation noise.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Drafting without a second model: Medusa heads and token trees
md: Not every tree method is lossless. Medusa's optional **typical acceptance** keeps a candidate if the target's probability exceeds $\min(\epsilon, \delta e^{-H(p)})$, a threshold that depends on the entropy $H$. It raises speed at higher temperatures but no longer samples from the target's distribution. Medusa-2 also changes the backbone weights, so outputs differ from the original model.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Word error rate: alignments, normalization and fair comparisons
md: Only compare WER numbers computed with the same normalizer on the same references. Switching normalizers, or counting *you're* versus *you are* as an error, can move WER more than a model upgrade. For languages written without spaces, character error rate (CER) is used instead.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The heap: free lists, chunk headers and where malloc gets memory
md: Stack: LIFO, bounded, freed by returning, one instruction. Heap: any order, any size, any lifetime, paid for with headers, rounding, free-list searches and fragmentation.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: Page faults: lazy allocation, copy-on-write and overcommit
md: Most page faults are normal: they are how Linux allocates memory on first touch and copies pages only on write. Count them with getrusage or `perf stat -e page-faults,major-faults`; worry about major faults and fault storms, not their existence.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: When steering fails: unreliable inputs and the prompting baseline
md: Steering is a research and monitoring tool before it is a product control. Use it when you need to know *which* internal direction drives a behavior, to detect a concept, or to add to a prompt (CAA's vectors still moved behavior on top of system prompts). Always report per-input effects, a random vector of equal norm and a prompting baseline; without them a mean effect proves little.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
md: End-to-end exactly-once needs three parts: a replayable source (Kafka offsets), consistent state (checkpoints), and an output that is transactional or idempotent (upsert by a deterministic key such as sensor and window). Duplicates created upstream, such as MQTT QoS 1 retries, must be removed by id.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Multi-head attention by hand: two heads, two patterns
md: Multi-head attention = several narrow attention functions in parallel, each free to learn a different pattern, at roughly the cost of one wide head.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Why raw TF-IDF ranks a keyword-stuffed page first
md: BM25 is still a sum over query terms of (IDF) x (a term-frequency factor). What changes is the term-frequency factor: it is bounded and length-aware instead of a raw count.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward
md: The causal mask is the only thing that makes this a *decoder*. Remove it and you have an encoder block; keep it and every position's prediction depends only on its prefix, so one pass trains all $T$ positions honestly.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
md: The derivative is not the change in $f$ over a big step. It is a rate at one point. For $x^2$ at 3, a step of $+2$ actually raises $f$ by 16, not $6 \times 2 = 12$, because the slope itself changes along the way. This is exactly why **gradient descent**, the training method that repeatedly moves every parameter a small step downhill (lesson 6), takes small steps.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: The multivariable chain rule: summing over every path
md: Multiply local derivatives along each path, then add over all paths from the input to the output. Fan-out in the forward pass becomes a sum in the backward pass.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Files, paths and permissions: finding your way around
md: A mode is nine bits in three groups of rwx (owner, group, others), written as three octal digits with r = 4, w = 2, x = 1. On a file, x means run it; on a directory, x means enter it. Exactly one group applies to you.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Searching and transforming text: grep, regex, find, sed and awk
md: `sed -i` edits a file in place, and it differs between systems. GNU sed (Linux) takes an optional backup suffix glued to the flag, so `sed -i 's/a/b/' f` works. BSD sed (macOS) requires the suffix argument, so the same command takes the script as the suffix and fails. `sed -i.bak 's/a/b/' f` works on both and keeps the original as `f.bak`.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Your environment and remote machines: dotfiles, ssh and tmux
md: Login shells read ~/.bash_profile, other interactive shells ~/.bashrc, scripts neither. ssh logs you in with a key pair whose private half never leaves your machine, and tmux keeps remote work alive when the connection drops.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Beyond words: autoencoders and the InfoNCE loss
md: Embeddings come from an objective, not from the lookup table. Pick the objective so that items you want close (words in the same contexts, two views of one image, a user and the items they clicked) are pushed together and everything else is pushed apart.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Fewer bytes per weight: number formats and weight-only quantization
md: Decode time per token is about weight bytes over bandwidth, so halving bits per weight roughly halves it. Weight-only quantization cuts bytes, not FLOPs: it speeds decode, not prefill.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Measure it: tokens per second, MBU and MFU
md: Compare every measurement with its floor. MBU near 70 to 80% at small batch means the bytes are the limit, so cut bytes (quantize) or add bandwidth (tensor parallelism). MBU far lower means overhead: launches, Python, unfused kernels.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Decisions in machine code: flags, compare and conditional jumps
md: Misconception: "the CPU knows whether a value is signed." It does not. `cmp` sets all four flags every time; the signedness lives only in which jump the compiler chose after it.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Virtual memory: every process gets its own addresses
md: Every address your program uses is virtual. The MMU translates it on every access using the current process's page table, the TLB makes that fast, and page faults let the OS fill in memory lazily.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
md: The reward model learns only from differences. Its job is to rank responses to the same prompt, and its output is a log-odds score: a gap of 1 means about 73 percent preference.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
md: Skip pointers only help AND-style intersections, where we look for a specific docID. For OR we must output every posting of both lists anyway, so there is nothing to skip. Skips are also costly to maintain when postings lists change often.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
md: C is small: a handful of types, operators that work on bits and integers as directly as the CPU does, and `if`, `for`, `while`, `switch` and functions. What makes it hard is not syntax but the rules for memory, which the rest of this course is about.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
md: A pointer does not know how many elements it points to. Whoever passes a buffer must also pass its length (or rely on a terminator such as the zero byte), and every write must be checked against that length.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
md: `void *` carries an address without a type; the code that receives it must convert it back to the right type. A function pointer carries code. Together they let one function such as qsort work on any data, with the caller supplying the type-specific part.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop
md: Ownership answers C's question *who frees this, and when?* statically: the single owner frees it, at the end of the owner's scope. No `free` calls, no collector.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs
md: Lifetime annotations do not change how long anything lives. They describe relationships between references so the borrow checker can verify each call site. The function body is checked against the signature, and callers are checked against the signature alone.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
md: A vector is an ordered list of $n$ numbers and also an arrow in $n$-dimensional space. Addition and scaling act component by component; the norm is the arrow's length.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b
md: $\det A$ is the factor by which $A$ scales areas (negative if it flips orientation). $\det A = 0$ means a direction is squashed flat: no inverse. Otherwise $A^{-1}A = I$ and $\mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{b}$, but in code you call `solve`, and you watch the condition number, not the determinant.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
md: A loss turns "fit the data" into one number that depends on the parameters. Squared error is the negative log-likelihood under Gaussian noise; cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood for class probabilities. Training means minimizing it.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Overfitting: when the training loss lies
md: Watch the **gap** between training and test (or validation: a held-out split used for tuning, see lesson 8) error. A small gap with high error means underfitting; a low training error with a large gap means overfitting. Training loss alone cannot tell you which you have.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Data pitfalls: leakage, distribution shift and baselines
md: Suspiciously good validation results are a bug report until proven otherwise. Check that every preprocessing step was fit on training rows only, that no group or time period straddles the split, and that no feature is recorded after the outcome it predicts.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The chain rule on a computational graph
md: Backprop = for each node in reverse order: upstream gradient times local gradient, summed over every path that leaves the node. One backward sweep yields the gradient for every input at once.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: Limited direct execution: let the program run natively, but first set up the hardware (trap table, timer, user mode) so that the OS always gets control back. A system call is the voluntary way back in; the timer interrupt is the involuntary one.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Waiting for something: condition variables and semaphores
md: Locks are for mutual exclusion; condition variables are for waiting until shared state changes. With a CV, always hold the lock, keep the condition in a state variable, and wait in a while loop. A semaphore can play either role, depending on its initial value.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
md: Data journaling writes every data block twice, which halves sequential write bandwidth. That is why metadata (ordered) journaling is the more common choice; OSTEP notes that Windows NTFS and SGI's XFS use forms of it.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
md: Linearity of expectation needs no independence, but the variance addition rule does. For dependent variables, $\text{Var}(X+Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X,Y)$. The **covariance** $\text{Cov}(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])]$, the mean product of the two deviations from their means, is positive when the two rise together and negative when one is high as the other is low. Lesson 8 develops it.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Bayesian estimation: priors, posteriors and MAP
md: With little data the prior drives the answer, so state it. A prior that puts zero probability on some value can never recover it: the posterior is the likelihood times the prior, and anything times 0 stays 0.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: $C \approx 6ND$. For a fixed budget, parameters and tokens trade off one for one in ratio: double $N$ and you must halve $D$.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
md: trec_eval ignores the rank column of a run file. It sorts by the score column and breaks ties by document id, so a run whose scores disagree with its ranks gets evaluated in score order, not the order you intended.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
md: Misconception: *semantic search understands meaning*. It finds vectors that are geometrically close, and closeness means whatever the training pairs rewarded. A model trained on question-answer pairs puts a question near its answer, not necessarily near a paraphrase of the question.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Training BPE: count adjacent pairs, merge the top one, repeat
md: The product of training is an **ordered list of merges**. Order matters: rank 1 is the first merge learned. The vocabulary is just the alphabet plus every merge result, and the next lesson shows that encoding new text replays this list in order.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
md: Tokenization fixes what the model can see. Vocabulary size trades sequence length against parameters; the regex and digit rules shape arithmetic; the training data mix decides which languages are cheap; and rare tokens can be under-trained.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Batch size, gradient accumulation and tuning hyperparameters
md: Accumulation is exactly equivalent only for layers that treat examples independently. **BatchNorm** computes statistics per micro-batch: with examples (1, 2, 3, 4) in one batch it normalizes the value 2 to -0.45, but in the micro-batch (1, 2) it becomes +1.00. The playbook also notes that accumulation gives no throughput benefit, since it runs the same small batches; it only changes the effective batch size.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic
md: Links are bidirectional when added, but pruning (step 4) can later drop a link from one side. The graph is therefore directed in practice, and a node whose incoming links are all pruned becomes hard or impossible to reach. Deletions are hard for the same reason; lesson 5 shows how libraries handle them.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Reproducible builds: proving a binary came from its source
md: Reproducible builds prove the binary matches *the source you built from*. They say nothing about which source that should be. xz 5.6.1's release tarball contained a malicious build script missing from git; rebuilding the tarball reproduces the backdoor perfectly. Compare release archives against the tagged git tree too (Arch Linux switched xz to building from git when the backdoor was disclosed).

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Reproduce collapse yourself: simulate the loops, measure diversity
md: A closed loop collapses at a rate set by the sample size, and you can measure that rate. A small but steady stream of real data turns the downward drift into a stable level.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
md: Treat 150 cycles as a floor from 2010 hardware, not a current number. Since then kernels added mitigations on every entry and exit for CPU vulnerabilities: you can see `SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3` (separate kernel page tables) and `IBRS_ENTER` (IBRS, Indirect Branch Restricted Speculation, limits branch speculation) in today's `entry_SYSCALL_64`. Measure on your own machine before quoting a number.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
md: The kernel's view of your memory is a list of VMAs. `execve` and ld.so create the first ones, `mmap` adds, `munmap` removes and splits, `mprotect` splits by permission, and `mremap` resizes or moves. `/proc/PID/maps` is that list, and it is the first thing to read when a mapping misbehaves.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Fan-out: why one server's p99 becomes everyone's problem
md: With fan-out N, the user-visible tail is set by roughly the 1 - 1/(100N) quantile of each component, not by its p99. A quantile is a percentile written as a fraction: the 0.99 quantile is p99. The formula is the N p at most 0.01 rule from the prediction, solved for p: each leaf may be slow at most 1/(100N) of the time. The wider the fan-out, the deeper into the tail you must measure and engineer.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
md: Derived numbers go stale. *Years of experience* computed at index time is wrong a month later for everyone with a current role. Store intervals with open ends and compute tenure at query time against the query's reference date, or recompute on a schedule and record the as-of date.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
md: These results are for one model family (PaLM 2-S*) with specially fine-tuned revision models and PRMs, on MATH. The qualitative lesson (match the method to difficulty; strong search over-optimizes a weak verifier) is the transferable part, not the exact 4x.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
md: A TTT layer is an RNN whose hidden state is a model. Update rule = train on the current token. Output rule = predict with the updated model. Choosing the model, the loss and the optimizer chooses the layer.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: After Titans: better objectives, optimal solvers, and replication
md: The successors keep the frame (a memory trained on a key-value loss as the sequence streams) and change what it fits and how well. A window or an exact solve protects earlier writes; a robust loss protects against outliers; forgetting decides how fast a changed fact wins. None of it is settled at scale.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: PEAK and TaHiTI: from backlog to handover
md: Both frameworks end the same way: a hunt is finished when its results are documented and handed to the teams that act on them. The query is not the deliverable. The deliverables are an escalation (if needed), detections, data and security recommendations, and knowledge for the next hunt.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The intelligence cycle and intelligence requirements
md: The most common failure is a collection-driven programme: buy feeds, read everything, publish a weekly "threat landscape" digest that supports no decision. FIRST warns that a meeting with leadership that is "informational only" will not go well. Start from requirements and work backwards.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Analytic tradecraft: bias and competing hypotheses
md: Weigh evidence by how well it *discriminates* between hypotheses, not by how much of it agrees with your favourite. Look for the item that would disprove each hypothesis, check its sensitivity, and always keep "someone wants us to think this" on the list.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Attack trees: start from the attacker's goal
md: The numbers are estimates and the tree is never complete. Schneier calls the safe example incomplete and warns not to read its values as a statement about how secure a real safe is. Use trees to compare options and find the cheapest path, not to claim an attack costs exactly 2,200.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: How Linux ranks nodes into tiers: abstract distance
md: Tiers are not the same as NUMA distance. A remote-socket DRAM node is far, but it has CPUs and DRAM-class performance, so it sits in the top tier and is never a demotion target for the other socket. Only slower memory types form lower tiers.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Prophet, the M4 competition and foundation models
md: Misconception: a bigger or newer model will beat simple methods. On the M4 data pure ML lost to simple combinations, and on our toy series SES with a fitted alpha was no better than naive. Any model, from Prophet to a foundation model, has to beat seasonal naive under rolling-origin evaluation before it ships.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Revocation: CRL, OCSP, stapling, and why short-lived certs won
md: "We revoked the certificate, so we are safe" is wishful thinking. Revocation reaches clients slowly and unreliably. Assume a compromised certificate is usable until it expires, and size your lifetimes accordingly.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
md: Autotuning has costs you do not see in steady state: the first call for each new `key` value compiles and benchmarks every config, and each distinct constexpr combination is a separate compiled kernel. Keep `key` to arguments that really change the best config, and use `prune_configs_by` to drop hopeless candidates.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Evaluating unified models and choosing a design
md: No axis is free. Discrete plus causal is the simplest to train and serve; continuous plus bidirectional plus separate encoders has led the reported GenEval numbers in these papers, at the cost of more moving parts. Pick based on what the product must do well, then evaluate both sides of the model.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Booting on the hypervisor: virtual devices, boot time and memory
md: Do not assume every unikernel does this. Sealing and compile-time randomization are Mirage's design; a 2019 study by the security firm NCC Group of two other unikernels, Rumprun and IncludeOS, found ASLR, W xor X and stack canaries (a random value placed before a function's return address and checked on return, so a buffer overflow is caught) absent or broken.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Graph traversal: memory layout, cache misses and prefetching
md: In graph search the expensive part per hop is often the first touch of a random vector, not the arithmetic. Contiguous fixed-size blocks, aligned vectors, prefetching and smaller (compressed) vectors all attack that same miss.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: One GRPO step through the V1 trainer, call by call
md: Read the source, not just the prose. verl's GSM8K example page says the scorer gives 0.1 for a well-formatted wrong answer, but in the current `gsm8k.py` the default `format_score` is 0.0 (the quickstart page also says 0.0). A silent difference like that changes what the policy is rewarded for.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Bigger context or captions: LongVA, Gemini 1.5, retrieval, benchmarks
md: Choose by the question. Sparse sampling plus pooling suits gist questions. Merging and memory banks suit streaming and bounded memory. Long context gives the most faithful view at the highest cost. Caption retrieval is cheapest per question and reuses work across questions, but only knows what the captioner wrote.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: I/O virtualization: emulation, virtio, passthrough and the IOMMU
md: EPT/NPT confines what the guest's *CPU* can touch; the IOMMU confines what the guest's *devices* can touch. Device assignment without an IOMMU (or with a group shared across tenants) quietly removes the memory wall from lesson 3.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Confidential VMs: SEV-SNP, TDX and Arm CCA stop trusting the host
md: A confidential VM moves trust from the host's software to the CPU vendor's hardware and firmware. It protects memory and registers from a curious or compromised host, not availability, not the guest's own bugs, and not data the guest sends through shared pages unencrypted.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Linear probe, LoRA or full fine-tune: choosing what to train
md: Decide by data and shift. Little data or a frozen-feature baseline needed: linear probe. Many tasks on one backbone or tight memory: LoRA (adapters are tiny and merge for free). Plenty of data from the deployment distribution: full fine-tune. Expect distribution shift at deployment: probe first, then fine-tune (LP-FT).

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Vector quantization: snap each vector to its nearest code
md: A common misreading is that the straight-through estimator makes quantization differentiable. It does not: it substitutes the identity gradient. The encoder is updated as if the decoder had received $z_e$, which is a useful but biased approximation that is better when $z_e$ stays close to its code.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Mixed prefill and decode in one forward pass
md: A mixed batch is one flat list of tokens plus offsets. Backends with one variable-length kernel use it as is. Backends with separate decode and prefill kernels ask for decodes first, so one index splits the batch.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules
md: Resizing is silent by default. If your receipt is downscaled, small digits may become unreadable and any coordinates the model returns refer to the resized image. Anthropic's docs recommend resizing yourself first; OpenAI's guide notes images may be resized even with original detail.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Herlihy's universal construction: announce, then help
md: The template for almost every wait-free algorithm since: **announce** your operation in a per-thread slot, then **help** pending operations in an order that guarantees each announced operation gets its turn within a bounded number of steps.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Scoring a forecast: latitude-weighted RMSE and ACC
md: Every global score is an area-weighted average. Weights proportional to cos(latitude) count each unit of Earth's surface once.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authentication: enumeration, lockout, reset and skipped steps
md: Lockout and reset tests act on accounts. Run them only on accounts you created. A lockout test against a real user's account is a denial of service against that person.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Writing a report that gets triaged, fixed and paid
md: Write for three readers: the triager reproduces, the engineer fixes, the lead prioritises. Exact steps with your own accounts, evidence, plausible impact, reasoned severity, a suggested fix, and no one else's data.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Content Security Policy: telling the browser which scripts to trust
md: CSP is defence in depth, not a fix. A permissive policy with `'unsafe-inline'` stops almost nothing, and even a strict policy cannot help if your own trusted script takes attacker text and passes it to `eval()` or builds script elements from it. Encode output and validate input first; then add CSP.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Access tokens and the access check: how Windows says yes or no
md: Because the walk stops early, ACE order changes the result. Windows tools keep a canonical order: explicit denies, then explicit allows, then inherited denies, then inherited allows. Hand-built DACLs in the wrong order can grant access you meant to deny.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Why a captured handshake allows offline password guessing
md: Changing the passphrase does not protect recordings already made: if an old passphrase is later guessed, every handshake recorded under it can be replayed into the PTK computation. With WPA2-Personal, the passphrase protects the past as well as the future.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app networking: cleartext, certificate checks and pinning
md: Leave certificate validation to the platform. The bug is almost always code that disables it: an empty trust manager, an always-true hostname verifier, a delegate that trusts any server, or a blanket ATS or cleartext exception. Pin only endpoints you control, and always ship a backup pin. Pins outlive app releases: NIST IR 8547 deprecates RSA and elliptic-curve keys after 2030, so plan rotation to post-quantum keys.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why cosine forces you to fix the training length up front
md: Cosine couples the **shape** of the LR curve to the **end date** of training. You must choose the training length before you start, and every checkpoint before the end is half-annealed.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: sendfile: from the page cache straight to the socket
md: sendfile shares page cache pages with the network stack. The man page warns that the transferred part of the file must stay unmodified until the reader on the other end has consumed it. If another process rewrites the file mid-send, the bytes on the wire can be a mix of old and new.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Prompting an LLM and calibrating its label bias
md: Two details. First, the bars show W p renormalized to sum to 1 for readability; the paper writes softmax(W p + b), which gives different numbers (T2 sports 0.911) but the same argmax, and the paper predicts with the argmax. Second, the bias is contextual: change the instruction, the examples, or their order, and p_cf must be measured again.
